synopsis: The market is modular: road-oriented tool chains are strong in sensors and scenarios but weak in soil physics, while heavy-machine physics tools are mature in dynamics, terrain and hydraulics but have thin sensor and scenario tooling [f195, f15860, f8290]. Braking-test quality depends on the machine model, which must include friction, slope, mass, payload, attachment position, tire or track state, and brake and hydraulic delay; implementation options range from point-mass models with lumped hydraulics to full multibody models with detailed plant [f15960, f15978, f6437, f6454]. Documented off-road options include Altair tracked-machine soft-soil workflows and Project Chrono 10.0.0, released on 27 March 2026, with wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles on deformable terrain; however, common handling tire models do not work on Chrono's deformable terrain [f6388, f8301, f8496, f15970]. A coupled renderer, dynamics, soil and HIL chain requires high integration effort, and heavy-machine vendors' sensor physics is not independently validated in weather [f13240, f15980]. No public apples-to-apples stopping-distance benchmark or evidence of toolchain superiority was found, and the skeptic's review describes Project Chrono as an unverified lead despite documented capabilities and research use elsewhere in the booklet [f6397, f6561, f6396, f11206, f15908].
